speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: DIPLOMATIC RELATIONS WITH INDEPENDENT AFRICAN STATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house is aware that the government has decided to extend its diplomatic relations with the independent states of Africa by opening two new resident diplomatic missions. On January 29 I informed hon. members of the appointment of the first Canadian high commissioner to Tanganyika, and today I am pleased to announce the appointment of Mr. Fulgence Charpentier as first Canadian ambassador to the republics of Cameroon Chad, Gabon and Congo (Brazzaville). He will be resident in the capital of Cameroon, Yaounde, with concurrent accreditation to the other three republics.
I am also pleased to announce that diplomatic relations have been established with the republics of Togo and Senegal. The Canadian high commissioner in Accra, Ghana, has been accredited as Canadian ambassador to the government of Togo; the Canadian high commissioner in Lagos, Nigeria, who is already accredited to Sierra Leone, has been accredited to the government of Senegal. This brings the number of African states with which Canada has formal relations to a total of 15. It is hoped that through arrangements for non-resident accreditation of our two Canadian heads of mission in Ghana and Nigeria, diplomatic relations will be established in the near future with additional French speaking states in west Africa.
The decision to establish diplomatic relations with these French speaking African states has been taken because of the increasing importance of Africa in world affairs and the growing influence of these states both within Africa and at the United Nations. The French African delegations have played a notably constructive part in the deliberations of the general assembly, and the Canadian delegation has worked closely with them on many issues. Sharing a common French cultural heritage, Canada and the French speaking states of Africa have a mutual interest in establishing diplomatic relations. The opening of diplomatic relations with these
countries will afford an excellent opportunity for strengthening these natural ties.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that this is a field in which Canada can render great service. In 1961 the government established an annual program for educational assistance to the French speaking countries of Africa, which the new mission will help to administer. Mr. Charpentier's appointment will give us a better insight into the problems and requirements of these countries, particularly in areas where Canadian experience will be useful.
Mr. Charpentier, a native of Ste. Anne de Prescott, Ontario, is well known on parliament hill and in the city of Ottawa. He was chief of French Journals in the House of Commons for some years and during the war was director of censorship, receiving the M.B.E. for his services. He was a controller of the city of Ottawa during the years 1932 to 1935. Since joining the Department of External Affairs in 1947 he has served abroad in a number of posts and is at present head of the passport office. Mr. Charpentier, who will take up his appointment shortly, will find that both French and English are used in Cameroon and therefore his proficiency in both these languages will be put to good use.

speechtext: I have a question for the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I wish to thank the hon. member for giving notice of his intention to ask this question. Mr. Speaker, I wish to address a question to the Minister of Veterans Affairs, as one old soldier to another, at the request of several other old soldiers in receipt of war veterans allowance. In view of the fact that the Department of Veterans Affairs is sending a notice to all recipients of war veterans allowance and widows allowance reading as follows: "The reduction in your war veterans allowance is the result of an equivalent increase in your old age security pension," would the minister inform the house whether he has received any protests concerning this policy? If so, is consideration being given to a review being made that would ensure that our older veterans and their widows, to whom we owe so much, are able to share this improvement in the pensions given to Canadians over 70 years of age?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the subject matter of this question is very important to a great many people. We have had some complaints due to a misunderstanding.
When war veterans allowances were first introduced nearly 30 years ago they were intended to be of assistance to those older returned soldiers who were unable to provide for themselves the necessities of life. It was felt that a number of former members of the forces, because of the arduous and dangerous nature of their service, had become pre-aged. The legislation was thus designed to provide financial assistance to service qualified veterans, in cases of need, at an age earlier than old age pensions become available to the population generally.
War veterans allowances were never intended to be paid independently of other sources of income, even where such income arose from war disability pensions or from pensions payable under social legislation. The purpose of the allowance is to assist those deserving and qualified veterans and their


dependants who are suffering from financial stringency, and in determining qualification for an allowance all other forms of income must be taken into consideration.
The result is that when those people who are of an age to receive the old age security pension get an increase in that pension, that is part of their total permissible income and is so recorded for war veterans allowances purposes. The war veterans allowance is not then as great as it was in the earlier month.
May I point out that it was only last year, just nine months ago, that the following changes were made in war veterans allowance. Previously the monthly rate for a single veteran had been $70; nine months ago it was raised to $84. The monthly rate for a married veteran was $120 nine months ago, and it was raised to $144. The ceiling for total income was increased, for a single veteran from $1,080 to $1,296 and for a married veteran from $1,740 to $2,088. In other words, a 20 per cent increase in the war veterans allowance was made effective June 1, 1961.

Mr. Speaker, a supplementary question. I understand the logic of the minister's reply to my friend the hon. member for Kootenay West, but is it not true that the statement just made implies the institution of a means test with respect to old age pensions to war veterans?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: The War Veterans Allowance Act has contained the so-called means test right from the beginning. There is nothing new in this at all. May I point out, Mr. Speaker, that there is the utmost sympathy on the part of this government for veterans and their dependants. The increase of last year which I mentioned was the third increase since we came into power with regard to war veterans allowance, and similarly the disability pensions were increased.

Mr. Speaker, may I ask a supplementary question. Does the minister not realize that the statement he has now made amounts to a formal announcement that the government does not intend to carry out another election promise?

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last evening I was discussing certain phases of the gross national product. I feel it is important to put on record figures indicating the gross national product in certain years between 1952 and 1960. In 1952 the gross national product was approximately $24 billion. By 1956 it had increased to $30.5 billion, an increase of $6.5 billion. By 1960 it had risen to $36 billion, and indications are that at the end of the present fiscal year it will stand at $37.5 billion. I point out that this figure reflects and bears a relationship to the loss of the wheat crop last year.
Mention has been made in this debate of the measures the government has taken to meet current problems. I cannot resist commenting on the quick action taken by the government last year with respect to the crop failure, the measures undertaken to provide financial assistance, to arrange for forage for cattle and to hold firm the market.
It is interesting that there has been a phenomenal growth in the gross national product despite the gloomy assertions placed on the record by hon. members of the Liberal party. I think it does no harm to review the facts. In 1957 when the Conservative government took office there were reasonable grounds for the gloom of hon. members of the opposition; not because we had taken over, but because they knew that in 1957 nothing could arrest the recession which had gradually been developing since 1955.
Who is rewriting history now?

The hon. member for Trinity asks who is rewriting history now. In reply I will fling in his teeth the frequently reiterated question: who caused the depression of 1930? The Liberals never heard of the depression of 1929 which was under way before the Conservative party came into power. They said we caused the depression in 1930. The Liberals formed the government up to that date and they were responsible for that recession. They were

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: You spent two years denying there was one.

It would do no harm to review the situation when we came in. There was tight money in 1957. Anyone who is familiar with conditions in his constituency at that time will know that tight money was in effect. Credit was tight and not available to the average businessman. Take another example, national housing. It was practically a nullity. There is no question about it. It was a case of try to get funds for national housing. They had it in the kitty; they had $50 million left over, but you could not get a loan. You could not get the thing processed. If you talked to any lawyers in your constituency at that time who handled these matters, they would tell you exactly the same thing, namely, "Sorry; we put in for a loan but we could not get them processed." They had $100 million, but if you examine the records now-and I will raise the matter later-there are $3 billion available for this national housing program. It is a matter of $100 million as against $3 billion.
Just to go back over this review, we had tight money, credit at a standstill, national housing at a standstill and our trade balance with other countries in a rather impossible situation-the Minister of Finance just put it on the record today-with $713 million of an imbalance, an alarming state. That is what the businessman was faced with when we came into office. Regardless of what has been said, there is no question but that when we came into office in 1957 we were obliged to take certain steps. It was necessary to do so for the economy of Canada. We took those steps. This government stepped right in.
As far as the over-all picture is concerned, we have long had a national policy which we are not backward in bringing forward. It is a policy which we talked about all along, and when the time came we put it into effect. Legislation was immediately forthcoming with regard to agriculture. I think it is fair to put on the record now what was done for agriculture in the last four years. Mind you, Mr. Speaker, they were rather tough years according to the Liberals. They are the people who have said those years have been bad. But despite all that, this government in the last four years has put in for agriculture twice as much as the previous government did in the previous four years.
The facts are irrefutable. I have mentioned national housing, which has been built up now so that housing is going ahead all over

the continent. The figure of $100 million has become $3 billion. In 1956-57 social justice payments stood at $1.3 billion. They have now become $2.3 billion, or in other words another $1 billion put out in social justice payments. Then as to dominion-provincial relations, they were improved immediately and the federal contributions all round have increased by 70 per cent over those made by the former administration. Those are dollars which have been put out to the provincial governments. There has been a 70 per cent increase. As to veterans legislation, we just had a brief rundown on that matter. Direct payments in the last year were up more than 50 per cent over those in the last year of the Liberal regime. In other words the figure which was $200 million has now become $305 million in direct payments to the veterans.
This is but a partial list. I do not wish to start throwing things down people's throats. However, I would recommend to members of the Liberal party or to any opposition member the admirable speech made in this house by the Minister of Public Works. It may be found at page 1155 of Hansard if hon. members care to look it up. That speech is predicated on achievements and promises fulfilled.
I like to look at my own riding in connection with this matter because we have heard criticism of deficit financing. Yet at the same time many things have been done. As to federal buildings, we have a federal building in the city of Penticton. It is a rather wonderful building. In my own home town of Oliver we have a federal building. Kelowna will have a new federal building. We have had post offices in Rutland and Keremeos. The R.C.M.P. barracks also. It is all part of a planned expansion program. There has been participation in health units and senior citizens dwellings. Incidentally, we have enlarged all the legislation with regard to those things.
In my own constituency breakwaters have been built on Okanagan lake, three brand new ones at Summerland, Peachland and Naramata, and there have been extensions and improvements to those in Penticton and Kelowna. In addition, one large airport has been put in and taken over by the Department of Transport at Kelowna. There is paving and reasonable lighting at the present time, and we hope to get more. At the city of Penticton there is an extension and more paving and an administration building. I name these things in order to indicate a few of the things we have done which were not on the shelf under the Liberal party, which were not there and available for this deficit financing. However, we went ahead in our

planning and we have benefited the constituency. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) spoke, as did the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) or rather the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey).
That is very different.

Yes, and a very different person also as a representative. If you read the speeches or if you listened to them as I did, I could not help feeling that the constituents were very well looked after. This is a part of a planned program of getting down to the people. I do not like to mention it here, but once again I go to my own constituency where we had cold storage subsidies in the last year alone of $345,000. That is a great deal of money. It is a great deal of aid to the growers of my constituency. It is a great deal of help to contractors all down the line. I have, of course, a little note here which says "And we have not finished yet". We have not finished by a long shot.
That had reference to the Minister of Public Works. The Minister of Trade and Commerce spoke yesterday. I would recommend that the opposition read his speech and take the figures, go over them and mull them over. In them they will see a great deal to chew on. They are good figures. They show the position of Canada. One thing that I thought was rather remarkable is the fact that the imbalance of trade has now been wiped out. For the first time in many many years we have a credit balance of trade with other countries, and we have this credit balance despite an increase in imports and exports throughout Canada.
There is no question but that we are doing very well. The businessmen of Canada and incidentally the press, barring Barron's Weekly, seem to take a fairly good view of that which is being done by the present government; in fact they take an excellent view. I know you will find the odd little Liberal press clipping here and there to wave around and say, "Look here", but the general thought is favourable, and this is the thought throughout the constituency. That is the important thing, after all is said and done, for one who knows the difference between the brass and the grass. If you know your grass you know that your own businessman is a fairly happy person.
I would also recommend the speeches made by the Minister of Labour. There is a great deal in them. I would particularly point out what was done with regard to the winter works program. Last year this government paid out as their portion of the labour costs in all projects the sum of $32 million. That is a great deal of money. That means that the
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth projects which were put into effect were rather large, when you consider them in total sums of money. Incidentally, I would point out that this is not a payment to the provinces, it is a direct payment to the municipalities on winter works. It is a direct payment in addition to all the other substantially increased payments which we have been making to the provinces and the municipalities in other forms.
The Minister of Labour mentioned vocational training. I think we owe him and the government a debt of gratitude also for putting that program into effect. In the city of Kelowna I am happy to say that the provincial government has seen fit to put up a vocational training school, and it is not going to be a small one. I think it is only fair to point out that this government is paying three quarters of the cost of that whole set-up. I have reference to the building or the fixed plant. It is only fair also to point out that certain other costs are shared with the provincial government. I refer to the cost of vocational training education. Furthermore, the cost of training teachers is shared as well. People do not seem to realize it, but the federal government has extended the act in order to give benefits to the provinces.

Strangely enough, there is criticism of the dollar discount on the part of Liberal candidates in the province of British Columbia. Some of them are even writing to the press about the matter. I have in mind my own industry, lumbering, which is the biggest industry in the province of British Columbia, and also the fruit industry, particularly apples. I can also say with authority that a mining boom has started in the province of British Columbia since the devaluation of the dollar, the like of which we have never seen before. In addition, all the little articles that are imported into Canada now enter with what might be called an additional invisible tariff barrier against them.

May I ask the house to go back in imagination to a period when difficulties were much greater than they are now, in 1962. I am going to ask the house to step back in imagination to the wartime cabinet of Great Britain in June, 1940. At that time the cabinet approved the final draft proclamation of an Anglo-French union and authorized its dispatch to M. Reynaud by the hand of General de Gaulle. This was on June 16, 1940, and the contents of the draft were telephoned to M. Reynaud. I wish to read extracts from that draft, and may I add that it was primarily the work of Winston Churchill, that gallant leader of Britain. It states:
At this most fateful moment in the history of the modern world, the governments of the United Kingdom and the French republic make this declaration of indissoluble union-
The two governments declare that France and Great Britain shall no longer be two nations, but one Franco-British union.
The constitution of the union will provide for joint organs of defence, foreign, financial and economic policies.
Every citizen of France will enjoy immediately citizenship of Great Britain; every British subject will become a citizen of France.
We might well say "ridiculous", yet in 1941 a man for whom I have the greatest admiration, Charles Morgan, a former professor at Oxford, gave two addresses, one in New York and one in London. In each he read the following:
It must be clear that the simplest law of selfpreservation requires that we have a friend and not an enemy in Paris.
But this strategical point is not the one I wish to make now. I put forward a different and more embracing claim-not that the strength and inde-pendance of France are necessary to our political survival but that the life and spirit of France constitute an idea the death of which would be the death of civilization. I have heard it said that France is decadent, that she is corrupt, that to the world of the future no good can come from her-
This was written on February 25, 1941.
-that the British empire and America can afford to do without her. I hold, on the contrary, that, in spite of her faults and failures, there is in her a unique element without which the energies and virtues of the Anglo Saxon peoples cannot yield their full fruit.
Of all the countries in the world, Canada is surely the one to support such a contention, to believe it and live by it. Winston Churchill, in his famous speech at Zurich in September, 1946 used these words:
Among the victors there is a babel of jarring voices, among the vanquished the sullen silence of despair. Yet all the while there is a remedy which would as if by a miracle transform the whole scene. It is to recreate the European family, or as much of it as we can, and provide it with a structure under which it can dwell in peace, in safety and in freedom. We must build a kind of united states of Europe.
When I was at the United Nations observing what was happening down there I noticed

And now suddenly this thing is happening. But what has been happening in all these years in Canada? About our attitude to these enormous changes of such far reaching importance culturally, economically, socially, affecting the survival of free people? This is one reason I so earnestly subscribe to the policies of the party to which I belong. I feel we must recognize that enormous changes are taking place in the world and that this unity of England and France-and of all Europe, indeed-is something that is ennobling to all mankind and in which we must participate in a vigorous way.
Can we not remember that when NATO was created the prime architect, according to the words of the chancellor of the University of London, was Mr. St. Laurent, who was then prime minister of Canada. It was our Mr. St. Laurent of Canada who had a major part in the formation of NATO, and it was certainly not thought in those days that NATO was something confined and related only to war. It was something very much larger than that.
Where do we stand on this matter? Our leader has expressed himself in rather clear terms, and I would ask hon. gentleman to listen for a moment. When the Atlantic trading community was first proposed by Lester B. Pearson in the House of Commons on March 21, 1960 the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) said:
There is no reason on earth why Canada should not at least associate itself in this initiative in an aggressive and formal way. It seems to me there is a real urgency in this matter. This is the time to do it if it is going to be done at all. The European countries are finalizing their respective trade arrangements and next year it might be too late for any alternative proposal to be made to them.
He spoke in almost the same terms to the Empire and Canadian clubs in Toronto on April 24, 1961, when he said:
This process of Atlantic economic integration must take place for political as well as commercial reasons. It is necessary for the prosperity and growth of the Atlantic democracies. But it may soon be necessary for their survival.
Then in the House of Commons on April 25, 1961, before I had the honour of being here, he said:
We should encourage European, economic as well as political integration on a basis of expanded, not restricted, trade, and then we should do everything we can to convert that European economic community into a political trade area with which, stage by stage, other free countries could be associated.

There are certain parts of Canada where they have caught the urgency of this. Certainly this is so in Winnipeg. A series of articles have been published in this connection. Max Freedman has written on this subject at different times, as has Maurice Western, who has written about "The Turtle at Ottawa." The Winnipeg Free Press has written repeatedly on the subject "Is Canada turning her back on destiny?", particularly in view of the great leadership that is now being shown by the present idealistic, energetic and courageous President of the United States.
Mr. Kennedy's state of the union message was by any measure a bold and masterly answer to what Mr. Fleming seemed to be seeking, a superb act of leadership in the face of formidable opposition in his own country and abroad, and it must have been with this thought in mind that five senior members of the American cabinet journeyed to Ottawa last week end in the confident expectation that they would find their counterparts in the Canadian cabinet enthusiastic about the president's program.
But according to the communique issued at the close of their talks the president's emissaries found nothing of the kind. "Canadian ministers," the communique said, "emphasized that the commonwealth trade links, including the exchange of preferences and the historic right of free entry into the United Kingdom market, were an essential cohesive element in the commonwealth association". Where the Americans came prepared to discuss the realities of the present the Canadians were able to speak in the platitudes of the past, delivering the same tiresome lectures with which they have been haranguing the British since the negotiations with the common market opened.
I submit that there is perhaps nothing more important and more exciting in political economy today than for us to think in terms of the sweeping changes that have taken place in the world since world war II. We know there have been various attempts in history, in the nineteenth century and indeed in the eighteenth century, toward a world community. We saw this with the British when they repealed the corn laws, and the subsequent sweeping movement towards new growth and development. It is noteworthy that there were just two countries which resisted this kind of economic development that was lifting mankind all over the world. There was Canada with her national policy of 1879, and in that same year Germany which moved in the direction of an imperialism which ultimately led to world war I.
We remember the chaos of the world community that produced world war I and later demonstrated itself in dangerous and insidious ways in the inflation of 1921 and 1922 and eventually the flight from gold. We saw France and Austria, and the United States pursue nationalistic monetary policies that were designed to do nothing but destroy the economic stability of the world and indeed most individual economies of the world.

But somehow or other we have got over that; at least we think we have. We think the world has been granted a second chance. In 1947 there was GATT and in 1950, through the energy of the French there was the Schumann plan. What a brave venture this was by the French with their old, traditional enemy Germany. We saw in O.E.E.C. a development in this direction. Finally these people determined that they could go a step further and there was the treaty of Rome which was finally signed in March, 1957 after much discussion and negotiation. In 1959 we saw the outer seven, led by Britain into the development of the E.F.T.A.
This is not only something that is happening in Europe. This is a movement, ecumenical in its concept, that is happening in other parts of the world. In our own hemisphere we found that in 1958 five central American countries under the leadership of Costa Rica were developing a customs union, and in 1960 there were seven other Latin American countries led by Argentina. This has all formed a great stepping stone to a future Latin-Amer-ican commonwealth which is certainly going to be in the nature of a great common market.
On November 2, 1961 our leader made this statement with respect to Atlantic trade. This was prompted by the Herter-Clayton report from Washington. The Leader of the Opposition said:
The Herter-Clayton report from Washington is of the greatest significance to Canada and all free countries. It would put the United States government right behind those principles of international trade that the Liberal party has advocated for a long time; principles that the Liberal opposition since 1957, have consistently urged on a Tory government in Ottawa, which has just as consistently ignored or rejected them.
Rather than collaborate with Great Britain in furthering these principles, in extending the European common market into an even wider common market, the present government has publicly upbraided and criticized the British government for moving in this direction. It has done this, even though it scorned a British offer of free trade with Canada made more than three years ago.
It is high time that our government awakened to the implications of what is going on across the Atlantic-and now across the border. It is high time that Canada's interests were promoted by positive and constructive policies instead of being damaged by the negative and sterile policy of the government.

For Canada 1961 may be remembered as the year when time ran out.
I hope this is not so. It seems to me that when we look fairly at the theories of political economy in this country, basically there is a

I think it may be interesting to examine the views of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce as set out in their 1958 report, giving their assessment of 1957. Under the heading "Canada's Fiscal and Monetary Policy" it is stated:
The year 1957, while a good year by most measurements of economic activity, and a record year for some industries, nevertheless registered a pause in the sharp upward thrust of the Canadian economy which commenced late in 1954. Over-all economic activity measured in dollars this year will probably be slightly above 1956, but in physical production will be no larger and possibly a little smaller. Demands on the economy remained strong in the early months of 1957, but towards the latter part of the year were less insistent, with inflationary pressures reduced, and many areas of business activity recorded declines from the corresponding months of 1956. Developments abroad were unsettling during the year. In the trade area

Britain and France experienced serious economic difficulties, and many raw material producing countries were adversely affected by the continued decline in commodity prices. In recent months confidence was disturbed by Soviet technological achievements, and by sharp declines in equity markets. Such developments, along with some weakness in the United States economy have created uncertainties which must be carefully assessed in appraising the outlook for Canadian business in 1958.
These people understand the Canadian business situation. They assessed it and were honest enough to recognize that the conditions referred to resulted not from the change of government but from what had happened in past years and the international situation. Referring to 1957 they state:
The past year has witnessed more cross currents in the Canadian economy than in any recent period. The inflationary pressures generated by the sharp advance of 1955-56 abated considerably as the year progressed, and by early fall money rates were receding from the high levels of the summer, reflecting less pressing demands for capital funds. On the one hand, shrinkage in external markets adversely affected exports of many basic products. Weakness was also noted in residential construction and in markets for some consumer durable goods.
Those in the Toronto area remember that at the beginning of 1957 there was considerable unemployment in the area, especially in the construction industry, because of the tight money policy of the former government. The then government did not make available to the industry the facilities at its disposal. Many people in my riding were out of work.
Some economists have just recently wakened to the fact that some of the difficulties of that period began to manifest themselves in 1958, but if they study history they will realize that the tight money policy of the former government in 1957 not only affected the construction industry but choked off the growth of many small businesses at that time. I recall many small businessmen who were planning developments in my area but could not proceed because of the tight money situation.
I wish to place on record a few passages from the Canadian chamber of commerce submission to the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue of February, 1962, which fairly assesses the situation in these words:
Exports have been buoyant enough to reduce the trade gap substantially, capital expenditures have held up fairly well, consumer spending in recent months has shown signs of revival and unemployment is gradually being reduced. Furthermore there are encouraging indications for continuation of the business recovery in the United States, always a good omen for Canada.
And later:
It is now evident in retrospect that Canada enjoyed exceptionally good fortune in the decade following world war II, and as a result of a

unique combination of circumstances forged ahead more rapidly than most other countries. This surge left its inevitable maladjustments, some of which may take as long to correct as they did to arise. The task of making necessary adjustments has been aggravated by the delayed emergence of many countries-particularly in western Europe-as keen competitors both in the markets of the world and in the Canadian market. There is no miracle by which the problems we face can be overcome in a day, but with the energetic and persistent pursuit of appropriate policies they can be overcome in the foreseeable future.
These policies must bring to bear all the imagination of business and government on a broad front, and must be directed toward increasing both consumption and capital investment at home as well as widening the market for Canadian products abroad. A judicious combination of fiscal and monetary policies, supplemented with other business and governmental measures, will continue to help materially in reaching these goals.
Then mark this statement, Mr. Speaker.
Fortunately, many of the programs that could be suggested have already been initiated.
As was stated, the executive council of the chamber of commerce accepts the extension of deficit financing into another year but with some reservations. Then further under "Tax Policy" we find the following:
The executive council wishes to commend the government for the steps it has already taken in the last two budgets to stimulate investment by an acceleration of capital cost allowances and to encourage research expenditures by the removal of past restrictions. These have been moves in the right direction. It is the view of the council, however, that more could be accomplished by giving greater incentives under existing programs, thus encouraging investment in more efficient plant and equipment that will operate at lower cost, and by the extension of measures to other areas, such as the export field.
Then again under "Monetary Policy" in the same report we find the following:
In view of developments of the last year which appear to have resolved some of the questions about which the executive council previously expressed concern and also having in mind that the royal commission on banking and finance will shortly be commencing its public hearings, the executive council has no extensive statement to make on monetary policy at this time. It would reiterate its firm belief in the necessity for close co-ordination between monetary, fiscal and other policies and in the desirability of maintaining flexibility in the monetary area in particular.
That is a slam at the government.
If the hon. member will wait I think he will find that they agree with what the government has done.
I say that is a slam at the government.

No. When I have finished what I am reading the hon. member may understand that it is a compliment to the government on what has been done. I continue:
The simultaneous requirements of a policy of easier money, of dealing with problems relating
Alleged. Lack of Economic Growth to a discount on the Canadian dollar and of assisting with financing the government's cash deficit will call for the exercise of greatest skill and imagination on the part of our monetary authorities in the months ahead.
Hear, hear.
We all agree with that statement, of course.
That is also a slam at the government.

The report continues:
The executive council expresses the hope that the developments of the last year, both in government and in the central bank, have brought about the conditions under which monetary policy will be able to fill the very important and exacting role which it is now expected to play.
In other words they agree with what happened last year, and the change. The report goes on to say:
The executive council commends the government for its energetic efforts to promote export sales through the expansion of its trade services and to increase productivity through establishment of the national productivity council. In the realm of trade negotiations-
And so on. It goes on commending the government for its activities in connection with trade. It states:
Our trade with the United States is vital to our economy and every opportunity of extending it should be explored. Finally, both the United Kingdom and the common market countries have indicated their willingness to participate in a program of tariff reduction on broad product groups. All these and other possibilities should be considered on their merits without slavish adherence to existing arrangements and in the light of the cold fact that without an aggressive and flexible approach Canada may find that it has suffered serious injury to its manufacturing industry and serious loss of its trade opportunities in the main markets of the world . .. The continuance of the discount on the Canadian dollar will also help to this end. The members of the government have given generous support to the need for exports by drawing attention to the subject frequently in their public utterances. It is hoped that this will continue and that the program will be encouraged by the adoption of further well conceived measures.
While recognizing that there is still a great deal to be done, that is the viewpoint of those in industry who have studied the needs of Canadian industry. Far from being pessimistic and far from being extremely critical, as the opposition has been, they have commended the government on the efforts that have been made.
They are Canadian.

That is right. We need to take into consideration in this matter not United States quotations which have been so glibly quoted in this house, but rather quotations from those in our own country. There is another quotation which it might be well to put on the record. It is from the commercial

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth letter of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce under the heading of "The Outlook for Exports":
During the year just past Canadian exports rose to new high levels. A feature of this increase was a marked improvement in trade with countries other than the United States and the United Kingdom. A high level of shipments was maintained to countries in western Europe, Asia and South America but exports to the United States lacked buoyancy until the latter half of the year when improvement in the third quarter pushed total exports to a record for that period-12.7 per cent higher than that of the same period in 1960.
As we know, for the first time since 1952 we have had a favourable trade balance. This was not something that happened just by accident. We all remember the early days, when the government proposed certain trade changes in order to be less dependent on the United States. The present opposition ridiculed that idea, and they have tried to becloud the trade issues today by casting an unfair reflection on the Canadian government and its attitude toward the common market. To hear them talk you would think Canada was the only country that was raising any question as to the implications of the common market.
Those of us who attended the commonwealth conference in London last year know that from every part of the commonwealth members rose and pointed1 out the adverse effects that entrance by Britain into the common market would have on their countries unless certain special preferences were given. Other countries, such as New Zealand and Australia, whose representatives have spoken just as strongly as have our ministers, have pointed out how their economy is much more directly dependent on their trade with Britain than ours, and they have said so in no uncertain terms. Nigeria and Ghana, whose major products are sold to Britain at the present time, would also be greatly affected by the entrance of Britain into the common market. India, which has based its new five year plan on the present trade arrangement with Britain, would be greatly affected by Britain's entry into the common market. They are very much concerned about what would happen to them. Even in England there are those who express concern about England's entry into the common market. Hon. E. Shin-well, a former minister in the Labour government, said this:
In 1959, we imported more than three times the amount from the commonwealth than we did from the Six. In 1960, we imported rather more than this amount. In 1959, we exported about four times more to the commonwealth than we sent to the countries of the Six. In 1960, we did rather better than in 1959-
At the same conference which we attended he expressed grave doubts as to England entering into the common market. One of the Conservative members also stated:

Of all those who have told me that we can go in and shape the community to suit our national purposes, none has ever said to me that we can go in on any other terms than on the acceptance of what is in article 3 about "a common customs tariff" and ''a common commercial policy toward third countries". It would split the Tory party were we to bind, beneath the votes or veto of a foreign or supranational agency, our liberty to arrange our trade with Australia, India, or any commonwealth realm or republic.
Michael Foot, Labour, said:
What we should do is to have the courage to recognize that we have still great associations with other countries that we can develop. We have not attempted to do it on anything like the scale that we should have done. Let us agree that this house and the British commonwealth should make the real decision.
Then Sir Norman Kipping, director general of the federation of British industries, said:
You will have seen, in the aide memoire to members about British industry and Europe approved ... by the federation of British industries, grand council, a significant sentence: "We will not support a solution which in effect meant that the commonwealth was to pay a substantial part of the price for British association with the common market". This is no expression of sentiment; it is an economic judgment.
As the hon. member for Leeds said, Mr. Speaker, it is true that these are challenging days. We must recognize changing trade patterns, but we must also recognize the implications of these and figure out as much as we can where we are going to fit into them. For instance, if Britain does enter the common market without being able to maintain the preferences in our favour there will be serious effects. For example, I understand that our refrigerators going into the English market get a 17 per cent preference. If Britain enters the common market we will lose that preference, and in addition we will have a tariff against us going into the common market of 10 per cent, which makes a 27 per cent difference in the tariff. That is something we have to take into consideration. Economically, are we geared to compete with this type of competition?
Then there is the political aspect. As I said recently in another speech in the house, with the assembly, the council and so on set up under article 3 or 4 of the treaty you have to abandon a certain amount of your sovereignty, and if the organization becomes a political union, as is the hope of the founders, where does the commonwealth go from there? Are we ready for that? Have we given any serious thought to the implications? Some have suggested that in the event Canada, as a result of natural trade trends, would become more and more a part of the United States and perhaps another state of the United States. These

are things that I believe we should be thinking about when we are talking about our national growth and where are are going. Nothing about that situation has been brought up by the opposition except for a compilation of statistics. You can use statistics to prove almost anything, if you want, but they have skipped around the major problems and the things we are faced with today. They have made no suggestion as to what we are going to do about automation and other things that affect our trade. With great relish they have quoted figures on unemployment, but this battle of statistics on unemployment is not going to give food or clothing to those who are out of work.
Hear, hear.
It is not going to give the person who is out of work the self-satisfaction and self respect he gets in obtaining a job.
Hear, hear.
I hear the hon. member for Essex East say "Hear, hear"-
We are waiting for action by the government.
-but all he does is quote statistics. In 22 years the Liberal regime, of which he was a major part, did nothing to prepare for the times we are faced with today.
The most prosperous period in the history of Canada.

The hon. member says "the most prosperous period". I will not deny that, but it was during those times of prosperity that you were blind to the trends that are causing our difficulties today. You did not see the growing chronic unemployment. You were bailed out of difficulty by the first world war, the second world war and the Korean war.
Tory times are hard times.
They are so blind today that they cannot see the new things that are being done by this party. They are still blind, and so are their economic advisers.
And so were the people of Canada for 22 years?

I agree that the people of Canada were blinded for 22 years by the hon. member's party. Perhaps at this time I should put on the record some of the things that the present government has done, just to remind these blind people across the way of what has been done.
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
They have doubled unemployment.
We have not doubled unemployment.
Yes.

We have inherited things that have caused unemployment. How can the people of this country be expected to go back to a party which has not yet learned the lessons it failed to learn in 22 years? First, the party to which I belong has greatly expanded the functions of the industrial development bank to provide small and medium sized firms with a larger source of working capital. Let the Liberals deny that. Second, we have made available loans to small business to provide working capital for those small but important industries which previously had no alternative source of funds for growth. During the tight money period started by the Liberals small businesses could not get money from the banks, while big businesses could.
Third, we have introduced accelerated depreciation to encourage the production of new products and the establishment of new industries in labour surplus areas. Fourth, we have set up a national productivity council to help industry to become more competitive and thereby increase sales and provide more jobs. Fifth, we have established a national design council to assist Canadian industries with their design problems by encouraging improved design to make possible more sales and more jobs. Sixth, in co-operation with the provinces the federal government is providing substantial assistance for the training and retraining of large numbers of the labour force. The object of this program is to prepare workers for the rapid technological changes which are taking place in Canada's industries. If Canada is to take its place as a modern industrial nation, its workers must have the skills to staff our modern factories.
There is something the Liberals neglected during the period they were in office. Today we lack certain skills in certain industries because they did not have the foresight to do anything about it except during the war. I will grant that during the war period they did help, but once the war was over that was as far as they would go. I know that in my own riding the government has authorized a new school, the Edith L. Groves junior vocational school, at an estimated cost of $1,211,000, and the federal government's share is about $908,250.

It was the province that authorized the school.

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
True, the province authorized the school, but at least the federal government offered the province assistance which was not given to them before.
Seventy five per cent.
Seventy five per cent of the cost.
Based upon an act introduced by a Liberal government.
That is right. They put a lot of inactive acts on the statute books, and this party had to put some life into them.
You mean you had to create unemployment?

You created it and we are trying to get rid of it. Perhaps I am unfair, Mr. Speaker, in saying that. I realize that world conditions did have some effect. I would not like to give them credit for being able to even create unemployment.
We also introduced the industrial promotion branch which has been created to help new industries become established and to expand old industries. During the past year there have been 12 meetings held with various provinces across this country. Representatives of these industries have sat down with government representatives who try to ascertain how conditions could be improved for the industries. There were three of them in Ontario which were very enthusiastic and who wanted to have these meetings.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member said we had done nothing. Of course we have done many things, only the opposition is too blind to see them. They are suffering from the same blindness that prevented them from seeing these problems accumulating while they were in power. I had hoped at this time to have some statistics to indicate the development of metropolitan Toronto. They do not appear to have come to my desk at this moment.
However, in closing-
There is a shortage of ammunition in the battle of statistics.

I just wanted to show that Toronto has been growing. We have been mastering the unemployment situation. However, there is still a great deal to be done. Before we take into consideration too much of what the opposition has said in the amendment before us, I should like to emphasize the fact that it was their arrogance and their tight money policy that led the people of Canada to vote against them. The present opposition had become fat and lazy when they were in power, and they had no economic policies. I think, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people will think twice before they

go back to this party which brought the people to the verge of the difficulties they are facing today.
The Liberal party has not learned very much since that time. In fact, Mr. Speaker, they remind one a great deal of the immature little boy who has been tripped and, in his rage, he starts kicking the thing that has tripped him. This is illustrated by the incident we saw in the house the other day when one hon. member turned and kicked the person who had tripped him, namely the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker). He started a personal vendetta against the man who had tripped him.
You are very critical today.
The hon. member says I am critical. I know I am usually quite calm, but after having heard the barrage of nonsense that came from the other side, I finally became aroused.
He was just quoting the Minister of Finance, you understand.

No, he was just misquoting the Minister of Finance. I place more reliance on what the Minister of Finance has said than on what the hon. member for Essex East has said.
A great deal was said last night about the cost of living index during the time the Conservatives have been in power. I think perhaps, in fairness, it ought to be shown that there was a little increase during the time the Liberals were in power.
More statistics.

That is correct; we have to fight fire with fire sometimes. If we left on the record only the statistics which hon. members opposite have quoted, perhaps the people of Canada might be misled, although I count a lot on the intelligence of the Canadian people. Between 1946 and 1948, the consumer price index advanced more than 25 per cent. This is one period during which the Liberals were in power. Then, with the outbreak of the Korean war in June 1950 came a resurgence of pressure on prices and in the course of the next 18 months further major upward movements took place. The consumer price index rose from 102.7 in July 1950 to 118.1 by December 1951, an increase of 15 per cent. Then between 1956 and 1957 there was an increase of 6.8 per cent. I put these figures on the record just to balance things up.
It is true that the cost of living has risen since we first came into power. The first year it rose more rapidly than it has latterly. However, these things happen in spite of

what may be done. I do not think they are to the credit or to the blame of any political party. I think the sooner that we, as members of parliament, realize this is more than a battle of statistics, then the sooner we will get at the fundamentals of the problems that are facing this country and the better it will be for the recovery and continued prosperity of the country.
Hear, hear.

I am glad hon. members applaud because this is the very thing we need them to recognize. I am sure that the things the government has done and will do, will aid the people of this country. I am not one who says we have done everything that can be done and that we have solved all the problems. However, at least this party is recognizing the problems and trying to do something about them, which is more than the Liberals did during their 22 years.

I found it very interesting to follow the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton). He referred to the 22 years the Liberals were in power, and that seems to have been a sort of theme song for the government backbenchers. I want to remind them of the solid basis that was created after the end of world war II. This government has seen fit to introduce measures which, in their relationship to the social and economic advancement of this country, have been merely the placing of one brick upon another, so to speak on a foundation created by the government of Mackenzie King.

This is not a new line of argument on economic matters such as we have before us, as was advanced by the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. Morton). We inherited troubles.
Yesterday the Minister of Trade and Commerce used the phrase "We have been in office for four and a half years." At the next opportunity the Canadian people put him out of office.
That was the greatest mistake they ever made.
They have just been complaining for four and a half years.

We heard from the hon. member for Davenport, who preceded me, that from a Liberal government we could expect a return to what he called a tight money policy. I do not want to deal with that at any length, but I do want to remind him that as a result of the terrible financial policies of his government the Canadian taxpayers on their federal debt alone are paying in interest more than $200 million more than what they paid in the last year of the former Liberal administration.
I want to say that the Minister of Finance cannot get away for long with gimmicks and sleight of hand, such as he introduced even in his most recent tabling of estimates. The only member of the government who has yet spoken is the Minister of Trade and Commerce, who spoke yesterday. He is of course a very cheery cheerleader for the government, but if one examines his speech he can find that it is not from this side but from the other side that one gets misleading statements.
I quote from page 1268 of Hansard where he referred to "the greatest prosperity this country has ever known." He also referred to an increase in exports of close to 8 per cent. I propose to deal with some of those matters. The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh), who has just interrupted me, referred to the phenomenal growth in gross national product and said that businessmen are happy in Canada today.
Now I do not want to quote from those who might have a partisan view. I shall refer to some appointees of the present government, and perhaps first and foremost would be the president of the productivity council. The hon. member for Leeds made reference to that this afternoon. I am not going to repeat some of the indications that are available as to whether this country has been growing or, on the contrary, getting behind under the present government. Let the figures speak for themselves. In terms of gross national product per person in constant dollars, using 1950 as 100 per cent, Canada shows itself as the losing team, limping sadly behind the competitive pack.
The hon. member for Leeds gave the comparative figures for various industrial countries of the world, and all these things have to be considered in relative terms. Rather than take a source in Canada, let us take one of major consequence in American investment. I refer to the Morgan Guaranty Company of New York, which looked at Canada's progress under this government. The hon. member for Okanagan Boundary (Mr. Pugh) says the government's programs have produced phenomenal improvements in our economic activity-
What are you quoting from?
The Morgan Guaranty Survey, reported in the Financial Times of June, 1961.

months ago.

We have here a motion of lack of confidence that the government in relative terms has not been advancing a program which is adequate to take care of the growth in our economy that would result in relatively full employment, relatively good tax revenues and relatively good progress. That is the essence of the amendment before us.
A subamendment has been put forward which reads in this way:
by the expansion of public and co-operative ownership for such purposes as the operation of utilities, the development of resources, the elimination of monopoly concentrations of power, and the operation of major enterprises immediately and directly affecting the entire nation.
Speaking for the official opposition I may say that while some of the wording of that subamendment is effective, we cannot support it because in our view it is undesirably restrictive of the main amendment. The main amendment says that by any possible form we must have growth. We believe that this growth would normally come from the encouragement of private business. We have never been loath as perhaps even our most understanding private enterpriser, Mr. C. D. Howe, has said, to have the state give the utmost stimulus to that type of growth.
What would he think of the hon. member for Assiniboia?

Emphasis is placed in the subamendment on the expansion of co-operation. Although this is important we do not believe this force would provide the greatest stimulus to the Canadian economy. We believe that incentives are required and that they would be most effective if applied to both public and private enterprise. The main emphasis to growth must come from healthy and vigorous enterprise throughout the economy. As we have indicated this requires planning beyond what this government is prepared to provide.
The productivity council has been in operation for a year and in my opinion has not yet reported in adequate form through a minister. I read yesterday that it is not an advisory board and has no authority. They deny all that. When the establishment of the council was announced in the throne speech in December 1960 there was much fanfare about the likelihood of its value. I hope a minister of the crown will tell us more about its usefulness and what it has accomplished, in a year particularly when it is denied that it

has authority of a kind we say would be desirable for an economic board or council within government for co-ordinating all the economic thinking and activity that takes place in so many individual departments and which at the moment possibly is not properly co-ordinated.
The other day I examined figures showing how much spending has been done by the government. I found that out of the unemployment insurance fund the following expenditures were made:

We can only surmise what the figure will be for the year ending March 31, 1962. It is now evident that the Minister of Finance will not present a budget this month. But let us be generous to him and assume the expenditure will not exceed $450 million. If that were the amount the total expended since 1957 would be $2,242 million. At the end of December last there were 601,000 claimants. The actual holdings and investments dropped like stones since this government came into office.
Someone said the other day that when they looked at the figures for only two years it was seen that we could have built two St. Lawrence seaways with the disbursements. The St. Lawrence seaway was considered a major project for Canada. What about the Chignecto canal? What about the second trans-Canada highway about which the Prime Minister spoke the other day in Edmonton? Is the government simply going to drop these sums of money in unemployment insurance like stones without thoughtful planning?
The chief and basic problem as I see it in the four and a half years during which the present government has been in office, with unfortunate results, arises from the muddle, squabbling and disunity that exist within the government and its lack of cohesion and leadership. Is it any wonder there is confusion in the-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Opposition.
-government.
Memories of the Quebec visit.
That was quite a comic opera of family rows and contradictions.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

With respect to almost any subject one could mention we can charge the
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth government and particularly the Minister of Finance and his department with confusing and contradictory policies. Where do we stand on interest rates? The minister has contradicted himself in every budget. What about the exchange rate? What about inflation? What about monetary policy? It is only a year ago the minister disclaimed any responsibility for actions and policies and then later decided to fire the governor of the Bank of Canada. In other words, we have had expedients rather than policies. This is the main roadblock to confidence in Canada today.
I invite the ministers of the crown to give us their opinions on a motion of this kind which is concerned with the growth of our economy. I invite them to give us information not only with respect to the productivity council to which I have referred but also with respect to the Bladen report.
In October a delegation from six communities where the automobile industry is established visited the Minister of Finance and indicated they wanted action and not eleventh hour decisions which are so typical of this government. There was no decision. Is there not something of consequence for our economy involved here? What about jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?
Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman be good enough to indicate what action he and his party think should be taken on the recommendations of the Bladen royal commission?
That was put on the record yesterday.

I feel the report contained much relating to the efficiencies of large scale production. That could be given some encouragement by the Minister of Finance. With unemployment as it is this winter the minister should not delay giving leadership. From October when the representatives of six communities visited him until now, no decision has been taken. He should not delay until he brings down his budget, which we know will not be brought down this month.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
speechtext: The hon. gentleman has not answered the question.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does the hon. gentleman support the recommendations of the royal commission?

In 1957 the Conservative opposition concentrated on the oil industry. When the Conservatives formed the government they decided to appoint another royal commission. Again they put in wraps an

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth industry, perhaps the only one which could have made progress and substantial advances at that time. This government is very enamoured of royal commissions. The Clark report on social security, a vital document, gathered dust on their desks for three years.
I ask the government how concerned it is about stimulating the economy in view of its record with respect to roads to resources. In January 1958 the government introduced a program concerning roads to resources of very much interest to northern Ontario. The government's partners in office in Toronto were so disinterested that unanimity was not achieved and no agreement was reached. Instead of building roads which would have required an expenditure of $1.5 million on the part of the federal and provincial government in this period of severe unemployment and at a time when future unemployment might have been arrested, it was decided all they could expend was $500,000.
I ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce who is absent at the moment why there has been so much dickering with respect to the uranium contract. Would this not lead to job opportunities? This is typical of the lack of leadership we have in this country at the present time.
Last year when the Minister of Finance introduced the budget we thought he was placing considerable reliance on a policy of devaluing the dollar. He indicated this would have the effect of assisting our export industries. How can that be reconciled with his firm conviction of a year previous that this should not and could not be done, that it represented a gigantic gamble? This is another indication of the confusion, contrariness and unpredictability which is responsible for the hesitancy some businessmen and exporters feel about having faith in the economic policies of the government. I refer to trade. The Minister of Finance is known to be a person who has great skill in the use of his hectoring manners. He can go to conferences and bluster, scream and so on. But the question I ask is this. Where is the good will upon which we can build trade?
The hon. member for Leeds referred to a speech made by the Leader of the Opposition in 1961, and in which he indicated that if another party was in power they would not create this iron curtain, would not adopt these tactics of wringing hands and screaming through key holes rather than joining conferences, but would participate in a serious manner in order to ascertain whether some of the great positive ideals of extending world trade could be fashioned with their participation. But from this government we have heard only of furtive restrictions against our best


customer, namely Great Britain. We have observed serious errors of judgment in connection with our trade arrangements with such countries as Cuba in reference to which, as will be recalled, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, "You cannot do business with any better businessmen". The Leader of the the Opposition has been joined by some extremely eminent and distinguished people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member will be fair enough to say that the minister who used that expression was frank enough to withdraw it later and to express regret. I am quite sure it is not worthy of the hon. member to refer to the original expression without also referring to the explanatory statement that followed.

Businessmen will be glad to hear that he withdrew it with regret. I do not intend to list all the company of people who belatedly, after the Leader of the Opposition spoke, saw some advantage in connection with our affinity with wider trade groups. However, the company is rather distinguished. I think of the president of the Canadian Pacific Railway and the president of the Montreal stock exchange. I think of Mr. Weston, one of our outstanding businessmen who also had some business experience overseas. I think of Mr. E. P. Taylor who also has extended his operations overseas. I think of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture. I think of the national chamber of commerce. I think of the presidents of the Bank of Montreal, the Toronto-Dominion Bank and the Bank of Nova Scotia, and there may be others.
On the part of the government we have had fumbling and indecision in connection with trade. I think trade is perhaps the only area of real value in which can be created new wealth which will give us the growth we believe necessary in order to provide employment and the progress which has not been forthcoming in past years when in relative terms, based on population and on a discount for the inflation which has taken place, this country has gone behind rather than forward under this government.
