Mr. Speaker, I was very much surprised to hear the remarks made by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Benidickson), because ever since the present government has been in power, the opposition has voted in favour of all the measures proposed to the house by the government, as well as the estimates that were submitted,

except the measure concerning Mr. Coyne's dismissal and another one to help Canadian industry.
In fact, I am astonished by the attitude of the members opposite. If they criticize today, they are not logical with themselves because they have voted, as I have just said, in favour of all the legislative measures submitted to the house by the present government; they have also approved straight off the expenditures of the present government.
I was also surprised by the remarks made yesterday by the hon. member for Niagara Falls (Miss LaMarsh).
I was amazed to hear her repeat those words of the late Right Hon. C. D. Howe:
If our national development had been left entirely to private enterprise, Canada would not have attained its present status as a nation. And unless government continues to take a lead by well planned initiatives, guidance and regulation, it will not continue to develop as it should.
Mr. Speaker, I found that when the Right Hon. C. D. Howe had to leave the realm of Canadian politics, he secured the directorship of more than 32 Canadian companies. In my opinion, the fact that he accepted all these appointments is directly opposed to the ideas he had put forward previously.
It was a tribute to his competence.

Mr. Speaker, the opposition speaks of economic planning. They would like to see the state control private enterprise, so that everything would come from the state.
During the last world conflict, we had a taste of controls and restrictions imposed by the state on our Canadian economy, when capital and salaries were under government control. Individual freedom was also restricted, as people were often detained without any kind of trial. Well, I think that the Canadian people are not ready to accept such a controlled economy, which would put everything in the hands of the state and, thereby, destroy private enterprise.
The state should rather assume a complementary part, while freedom of expression and freedom of investment in our natural resources must be left to the individual.
Mr. Speaker, I have here the encyclical issued by His Holiness Pope John XXIII, entitled Mater et Magistra, from which I quote the following paragraph:
Socialization is, at one and the same time, an effect and a cause of the growing intervention of the public authorities in even the most crucial matters, such as those concerning the care of
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
health, the instruction and education of the younger generation, the controlling of professional careers and the methods of care and rehabilitation of those variously handicapped.
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, who is so frequently mentioned in this house and who was at the helm of this nation's economic affairs for many years, unfortunately did not have any vision with regard to this country's future.
Indeed, when, during the war, billions of dollars were spent on national defence, it would have been easy for him, I think, to conceive and prepare a program for post-war years. As a matter of fact, unemployment was certainly expected, since the unemployment insurance fund was created at the time.
Mr. C. D. Howe should have gazed into the Mackenzie King crystal ball to find means of setting up a program to help Canada's postwar economy.
Mr. Pickersgill had it.

Mr. Speaker, various commissions were established by that government, especially the Gordon commission which recommended that the people of the maritimes be given one-way tickets out of the Atlantic provinces.
The previous government did not have any confidence in the future of the maritime provinces, but the government of the day has, by its policies and its action, taken steps to hasten the expansion of the maritimes and it will keep on doing so.
Mr. Gordon's comments were an insult to the people of Canada and especially to all those living in the maritimes. Fortunately, Canada will never put its destiny in the hands of men like Messrs. Gordon, Pearson, La-montagne and Pickersgill because it does not want to suffer again from the kind of planning it experienced under the previous Liberal government, that is belt-tightening policies.
Mr. Speaker, at the same time, they were lending millions of dollars for the construction of a pipe line in Canada.
Since 1957, Canadian exports have increased by 10 per cent, while our imports have decreased by 3 per cent.
May I be allowed to refer to an article published in the Sherbrooke newspaper La Tribune, which reads as follows:
In the field of international trade, Canada must face strong competition from countries where the cost of producing articles we export is lower than ours. Until now, we have managed to hold our own inasmuch as the increase in the cost of raw materials and labour has been offset by an increase in productivity, but this achievement is becoming more and more difficult.
1318	HOUSE OF
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
This situation is causing grave concern in many circles which are well aware of existing conditions. Warnings have already been sounded, pointing out the danger for Canada of finding itself excluded from international outlets because of its inability to put products on the market at the same price as those offered by other exporting countries.
We are already affected by those circumstances at home and some industries find themselves in a critical position because of stiff competition from abroad. Exports are of vital importance to Canada and that importance is emphasized by the fact that our country ranks fourth among the trading nations of the world. A few days ago, the president of the Royal Bank of Canada warned his fellow-citizens and said that we had to expect that not only the Russians and Chinese but also other Asiatics and Africans would be in a position to offer manufactured products at bargain prices.
To meet that competition we will have to take the measures required: we must increase productivity and cut down production costs with all the sacrifices involved for the manufacturers and their employees. Otherwise we shall run the risk of being cut off from world markets, which could have serious effects on our prosperity.
I believe that it would be fair for labour, when negotiating the renewal of work agreements, to consider not only its own problems but also the fact that its action might have repercussions on the economy of this country.
Mr. Speaker, it is also appropriate, I think, to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce to continue his efforts in order that Canada may have exhibits at international fairs. This is excellent publicity. In that respect, we should follow the example set by Japan which conducts intensive publicity throughout the world in order to sell its products. We should also encourage the Minister of Trade and Commerce to send, every year, trade missions throughout the world to make the economy of our country better known and to promote the sale of our products.
It would be a good thing also that the number of Canadian industrialists on those trade missions be increased and that a greater number of French-speaking industrialists join them, since there is a great number of Frenchspeaking industrialists in the province of Quebec who would be happy to show their products abroad and thus contribute to the expansion of our external trade.
As far as agriculture is concerned, farm income reached a record level in 1961. Economists foresee the same thing for 1962. I wish to refer here to a speech made at the convention of the Cooperative Federee de Quebec, which was held at Mount Royal hotel in Montreal on the occasion of its 40th


annual meeting. The convention was attended by 1,200 people. I quote:
Mr. Nadeau emphasized before the meeting that co-operative production plans are a sure means of raising farm income, since they are meant precisely to increase the net revenue of farm operators, to enable them to take better advantage of their own markets and to supply consumers with quality products.
Those words are not mere wishful thinking. In fact, with the exception of a few dairy products and barbecue chickens, most other farm products do not meet the needs of the people of the province. Quebec, which consumes 29 per cent of meat production in Canada, accounts for only 12 per cent of that production.
Thus last year, when there was a demand for 1.9 million hogs, only 1.5 million were marketed while 200,000 were imported. If the present rate of increase in population and the present rate of pork consumption per capita are maintained, the demand will be 2.1 million hogs in 1966 and 2.4 million in 1971. Which means that if production is to reach the level of consumption in 1971, production will have to be doubled between now and then.
Also, out of a total market of 125 million dozens of eggs in 1961, which will increase to 140 million dozens in 1966 and to 157 million dozens in 1971, Quebec produced only 62 million dozens in 1961.
Roughly speaking, it is the same story with regard to the production of turkey, lamb, beef and even veal.
On the other hand, co-operative plans are not new to co-operatives. Co-operatives have always brought under the same control, that of the farmers, the production, processing and distribution functions. The joining together of the means of action of a great number of small farms provides them with a great strength on the supply and farm product markets.
Finally, concluded Mr. Nadeau, production cooperative plans offer advantages both at the producers' level and at the local and central co-operative levels.
Mr. Speaker, it is important that Canadian farmers do not rely only on the state to increase their income. The state must help farmers, it must play a complementary role. I believe that one of the best means farmers may use to help themselves is to organize themselves through co-operatives, which are the ideal method for the controlling of production and for ensuring a stable income to Canadian farmers.
The present government has done much for all Canadian farmers.
According to the statement of the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier)-a statement made outside the house of course-the Canadian government is giving everything to western producers and nothing to eastern producers. I consider that statement as untrue. The hon. member for Laurier would be ashamed to repeat those words in the western provinces.

Mr. Speaker, the present government is responsible for the increase of the floor price on butter from 58 cents to 64 cents per pound, which was put into effect to help our farmers.
When the U.C.C. was coming to Ottawa to submit its briefs to the then minister of agriculture, the government chose to ignore its briefs as well as those that were submitted by the Cooperative Federee. A subsidy of 25 cents per hundred pounds of milk has also been granted to our producers, under certain conditions. From 1959 to 1960, out of nearly $11 million handed out by the Canadian government for all the provinces of Canada, almost $5 million have been paid out to the farmers in the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, the present government has been of great assistance to our Canadian farmers. Under the previous administration, the Canadian farm loan ceiling was $15,000, and loans could not go beyond 65 per cent of the value of the farm. Under the present administration, the loans range up to $20,000 and even $27,500, and they are accepted up to 75 per cent of the value of the farm.
Mr. Speaker, as my riding is a tobaccogrowing centre, I wish to underline the fact that since July 1959, a special duty of 75 cents per pound is levied on synthetic binders imported from the United States. This duty has been imposed in order to assist the cigar tobacco industry in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, the government of the province of Quebec also has its responsibilities as regards agriculture.
I notice that the order passed by that government concerning wood, and which gives the producers $11 per cord-

Allow me also, Mr. Speaker, to point out a situation that prevails now in the province of Quebec and which will surely affect the agricultural economy of this country; I refer to the provincial government's decision to refuse a higher school of agriculture to the Montreal district.

Mr. Speaker, I just wanted to draw attention to that question, because it affects the agricultural economy of the province of Quebec and of the country. However, I shall bow to your ruling.
There was also some mention of loans to be offered to municipalities. The federal government has some kind of a bank to grant loans to municipalities. We should think twice and use caution before implementing such a formula, so that it does not conflict with provincial autonomy, since municipal affairs are a provincial responsibility.
I wish to congratulate the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) for having extended, following the requests of Canadian municipalities the period provided for the winter works program. All those measures are a contribution to the country's economy.
There is reason to rejoice, Mr. Speaker, over the decisions reached by the Canadian government in the various fields of our economic activities.
As I said earlier, our opponents across the aisle, even though they criticized and made gloomy contributions to the debates of the house, have nevertheless supported all the leglislation introduced by the government and all the estimates, except in two instances.
(Text):

We are
concerned this afternoon with an amendment dealing with the problem of economic growth. I think this debate has shown up the extent to which we substantially differ on how this can be achieved. I think I can agree with the hon. member for Niagara Falls that this will be the central issue in the coming election campaign because all other matters revolve about it. We cannot have full employment without economic growth. Our welfare policies, old age pensions, veterans pensions, and all the other means by which we transfer money from one group to another will be of no account without economic growth. Our foreign policy and our defence commitments can both be seriously weakened unless we have economic growth. Even our hopes for a better trained and more skilled working force can be destroyed unless we can achieve this kind of economic growth.

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth
We are, therefore, dealing with a very important decision. One of the former statesmen of this nation suggested that the twentieth century would belong to Canada. Well, we will have to make a decision very soon, within the next few years, or I am afraid we will have to revise that statement quite substantially. The New Democratic party believes that this goal can only be achieved by long range planning, and that the greater part of this planning must be done at the federal level. We believe that it must be done democratically. We believe that in every stage the planning should be under the scrutiny of the people and their representatives in this parliament. We believe this planning must be done with the co-operation of all concerned, of management, labour, farm and the consumer. All these people have a right to play a part in it.
Finally, we recognize the over-all responsibility of the representatives of the people gathered in this parliament in the formation of the actual goals to which this planning can be directed. In other words, the New Democratic party believes that democracy has an economic as well as a political connotation. Until this is an accepted part of our system, political democracy itself could well be in danger. I was very much interested last night in the speech by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey). He is always interesting. One of the remarks he made was that we must now allow the state to undermine the role of the individual. I believe my political party can agree with this because we believe that the individual can only work properly when the state itself provides the opportunity.
It has been said of this government by its spokesmen that it does not believe in planning. It believes rather in slogans; that the issues confronting this nation are those revolving about the distinction between free enterprise and socialism. The fact that a minister of the crown could make such a fantastic statement and not be laughed off the stage shows how far we are behind in our thinking about social and economic issues. In Europe, they stopped talking about socialism. They have stopped worrying about socialism and gone to work to deal with their economies which are moving ahead to provide the kind of growth which we in Canada need. They realize that the terms "socialism" and "free enterprise" are completely irrelevant in the twentieth century. How we in Canada with the Canadian National, Trans-Canada Air Lines, the national film board, the C.B.C. and Polymer, with our dominion coal board, the fisheries prices support board and the

national research council, can talk about free enterprise, is indeed a mystery.
I am reminded of a little town not far from Ottawa. Sometimes in the summer I visit this town. There is not a single industry there and even the cheese factory has closed down. The railway trains do not even stop at the station any longer, but simply flash by. I wondered how these people actually lived, how they got along. I found out. At the end of the month, in came all the family allowance cheques, the old age pensions, the veterans pensions and the other various transfer payments we have in this nation. Of course, we agree with those. It is rather interesting, though, to note that in the last election every single person in that town but one voted for the Conservative party. This person was a postmaster who had been appointed during the Liberal regime. I suppose in the next election these people will go to the polls again and vote for the Conservative party, free enterprise. Well, this is the kind of dichotomy of thought we have in this country. I think it is an extremely strange thing indeed, that we are still talking about socialism and free enterprise. Well, of course, according to the philosophy of this government it is easy to be right, it is easy to be successful, because there is no basis for assessing either success or failure. There are no goals to attain and therefore there are no goals to miss. One would have to agree with a quotation from a little book I found recently in the library entitled "Undirected Society". It reads thus:
The politician works among variables so numerous and so uncertain that his most brilliant insights can never be proved right and his grossest blunders proved wrong.
And so this government takes refuge in statistics as a giant curtain to hide the obvious.
We are told by the Minister of Trade and Commerce that there are more people at work than ever before. Obviously there are because the population is larger. Could you imagine the chaos if that situation did not exist? However, the government does not mention that there are more people unemployed now than in the 1930's, and the Minister of Trade and Commerce did not mention the social problems that this has created in many parts of Canada. He did not mention that in one city alone welfare is up 180 per cent over the previous year.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce told us that the gross national product is 22 per cent higher over a four or five year period, but does he not realize that the gross national product could be 100 per cent higher in 20 years time, and we could still have two thirds of our population unemployed? The only relevance his statement would have is

simply that technology has moved ahead; but we have not moved ahead in learning to provide employment. Thus we continue tinkering away, refusing to believe that the human mind can bring order and progress in areas of economics and social welfare as it has in so many other areas.
This element of economic growth is very important at this particular time because we have never been so conscious of the new trade patterns which are developing throughout the world. In many countries, including those in the European common market, there has been an acceptance of a much greater amount of government initiative and direction. They have set goals. They have set national goals and, indeed, international goals while we blither and mumble on about free enterprise.
We in Canada talk apologetically about a full employment society while these countries already have that. We talk about the possibility of a police state, should we try to set up a full employment society, at the same time forgetting that Great Britain, West Germany and many other countries have already achieved that objective. What other kind of society can we have? How can we compete with these countries when we have 7, 8, 9 or maybe even 11 per cent of our people unemployed during the winter months?
Let us look at this very dispassionately. Let us forget the amount of social welfare we pay at present to these people who are unemployed. Instead, let us remember we made a decision some time in the 19th century that we were going to keep people alive and not let them starve; that we were going to pay for them to eat and to be clothed and housed whether they are working or not. We decided that, and our Christian conscience demands that they be clothed and housed in a decent way, and kept at a level of subsistence which we could accept in our western civilization.
Once this decision is made, surely the only thing we have to decide is how we are going to implement it? When we ask ourselves that, we find we have only two alternatives left. We can allow them to become productive workers or we can allow them to be unemployed and be a drag on our whole economy. We can allow them to bear the cost of government and bear the cost of those things we regard as being necessary to our way of life, or we can allow them to take out of society what they must have in order to survive. Those are the only two alternatives we have. In fact it is only a matter of organization once you make your basic decision.
When he spoke yesterday, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said with some pride that for the first time we have a balance of
Alleged Lack of Economic Growth trade. Is that the only thing we have to be concerned with-a balance of trade?
Only in commodities.

Yes, a balance of trade in commodities; but that does not answer the major problem. The fact that we are trading wheat for transistor radios raises the point of the employment provided. I may say we are all very glad to see the wheat being sold, but I am sure all of us realize that the labour content of our exports does not in any way compare with the labour content of the imports we are bringing in. I think we should be more concerned about the level of exports which we have in manufactured products, a field in which we are far behind Italy, West Germany, Sweden and Switzerland. By exporting more manufactured products we are going to produce more labour and we are going to keep our people employed.

speechtext: Would the hon. member permit a question? What does he propose? How does he propose to deal with the problem?

I am sure if you read our program you would find out. We believe in a far greater measure of social investment and in encouraging far more employment right here in Canada. We would also be interested in expanding trade as much as possible by giving low interest rates, credit and so forth. This was no group of wild-eyed radicals who wanted to create prosperity. The group mentioned in the article included the Quebec federation of labour, the confederation of national syndicates, the provincial chamber of commerce, the Catholic farmers' union and the professional association of industrialists. These are the men who are suggesting planning and among them are supporters of the present government.
I was also interested in some remarks made by Mr. W. S. Kirkpatrick, president of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, whose name has already been used in this debate. He has been reported as suggesting the establishment of a federal group to accelerate expansion, a federal department of economic expansion. You see, you cannot set goals without planning, and according to Mr. Kirkpatrick we must do so in such a way as to accelerate the country's expansion and keep all Canadians working. He says:
Such a department should not be an adjunct of an existing department but a separate ministry headed by a senior cabinet minister.
It should have an advisory body, including the best brains of the country, drawn from business, labour, agriculture and academic circles, but selected as private citizens for their knowledge and experience and not as representing any group or organization.
In consultation with this advisory group, the new department would have the responsibility of developing general economic policies, and other government departments would plan their actions within the policies so established.
It is interesting to follow the chamber of commerce and to view some of its latest pronouncements. I was interested in the remarks of Mr. E. P. Taylor who recently made his first speech in 16 years. What did he suggest? He suggested a "big daddy" on economics. I shall quote from the Toronto daily Star which carried the following article:
Toronto's E. P. Taylor last night called for a federal "big daddy" to oversee the whole field of finance and trade.
In an interview following his first public speech in 16 years, he said such a man should be responsible for several departments, including finance, trade and commerce, national revenue and labour.
In his 40 minute speech concluding the Canadian Chamber of Commerce annual meeting, the president of the Argus Corporation got closer to the heart of Canada's ailing economy and came up with more concrete proposals than 650 delegates in three days of floundering.
The speech was based on on-the-spot reports by two economists hired by Mr. Taylor to study economic trends in Britain, France, West Germany and Sweden.
-he proposed the formation of a new federal cabinet post-minister of economic affairs. The minister, he says, would be a kind of "big daddy" over several departments-


It is almost Orwellian in its nature, if one remembers "Big Brother". He added:
This man would be able to draw in people from business, industry and labour and put their heads together.
The Germans have done this, and the French in a different way. This is one of the main reasons they are getting things done over there.
So says Mr. Taylor, but the labour movement has recognized this, and some time ago in his annual statement, Mr. Claude Jodoin stated:
We suggest that the time has arrived when the appointment of a social economic advisory council should be effected as the first step toward a better relationship and a united attack on our economic problems.
We sincerely believe there is a need for planning by this government, and the second major problem is also associated with trade. It is the problem of productivity.
We are told that our prosperity depends on our productivity. We can see the need for this but what will be the effect on the entire nation, on those who are not going to receive the benefits of this productivity? We have a productivity council but how can labour be very enthralled if productivity means fewer jobs? Only by a national effort at productivity in which management and labour can see the advantages, can we achieve this. Labour must not be placed at a disadvantage.
Some days ago the Minister of Labour expressed dissatisfaction that there was a labour management committee in existence but no meetings had been held. It would be pointless to hold them, to get them together, when this government is against planning. There is no pattern into which they can fit their plans. There is no point in planning and getting together unless they know where the government is going, and certainly there is no way of being certain of that.
Just a little over a year ago there was a great gathering of the economic leaders of our nation in Ottawa. They met, presented their reports and went home. What came of it all? Perhaps some of its work found its way into legislation but certainly those who attended the meeting do not feel their suggestions have been given proper credence by the government.
There can be no assurance about the benefits of higher productivity unless the government takes a hand. There can be no assurance given especially if it means less work for more people. Unless it means general prosperity and not simply unemployment insurance plus higher profits, no assurance can be given. Neither the unions nor businessmen are going to place themselves at the mercy of unplanned inaction such as we have today. We feel the government is elected by the

people. It is the only democratic agency but it cannot play any part in electing union and business leaders.
Therefore we believe that the government has a responsibility to take hold of and take a hand in the economic affairs of this nation. We believe that the rights of the minority must be guarded and the rights of property must be respected, but we also believe that the rights of the majority deserve some respect and that the rights of the consumer and those people who are in distress, those who are aged or sick, must be respected.
The third1 program is also associated with trade. A few articles appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail some weeks ago which indicated that Canada is going to find it harder and harder to compete in trade unless she begins to merge some of her industries; unless somehow we stop the fragmentation and allow the building up of much larger units of production. This was brought out in an article by Bruce Macdonald in which he said, quoting Humphrey Style, president of the John Inglis Co. Ltd.:
It seems to me that part of our national policy should be to encourage mergers into larger units to get the cost advantages from greater volume of production and distribution.
It may be that to achieve this greater degree of integration, while at the same time protecting the interests of the public in assuring them that the resultant cost advantages are passed on to them, some degree of modification of our existing anticombines legislation and its implementation must be made.
Mr. David Henry, director of the combines investigation branch of the Department of Justice, substantiated this view in saying:
In considering the implications of any particular merger the director is acting under the same disability that faces legal and economic advisers of industries planning to merge, namely that there is as yet very little jurisprudence that can serve as a guide as to how courts will view the legislation in light of particular circumstances.
So we are faced with the problem of having to plan great mergers, but how can this be done unless we do it within the pattern of a planned economy? How can we be sure that these mergers that we may have to allow to be formed, if we are going to compete for markets, will not mean monopoly prices, higher profits and once again appalling unemployment, unless there is some pattern of social justice in all the democratic planning with which this third program is concerned?
I read the speech of the hon. member for Niagara Falls and I am rather disappointed that the Liberal party is not going to support the amendment to the amendment proposed by this group. We in this group are rather surprised and sorry that the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) is not here to

I think he would be rather concerned to find that his political party is not accepting this particular amendment to the amendment proposed by the New Democratic group in this house.
I wish the Liberal party could accept this amendment because I am afraid that planning without such an amendment and without its emphasis will become a kind of research activity. It can too often become a tossing around of the ball. But surely decisions must be made somewhere, and the proper people to make the decisions are those who are elected democratically to make them. As it is now, of course, these decisions are made by stockholders, and rightly so. They are made on the basis of the best profits that can be secured for the stockholders-and why not? AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I was indicating that from the point of view of the New Democratic party, to achieve the kind of economic growth which is suggested in the amendment and subamendment it is paramount that some degree of responsibility be accepted by the federal government. I attempted to point out that there are several significant problems confronting the Canadian people today. These are problems of major proportions which must be dealt with within the near future or perhaps the opportunity to deal with them will pass.
The first problem is that of new trade competition, the competition provided by countries the governments of which have accepted a higher degree of responsibility and initiative and insisted on a full employment society.
The second problem is that of productivity. We face competition from nations which have recently engaged in a tooling up in industry on a large scale and in a modem way. We

Alleged Lack of Economic Growth cannot face this problem of productivity unless management, labour and indeed agriculture can feel they, too, will share in the benefits of productivity. Perhaps the farmer more than any other individual has already experienced disadvantages from productivity. He was told all he had to do was increase his production and his life would be one of considerable prosperity. As it turned out, of course, this was not true. His prices went down, his income continued to decline. Fewer and fewer are being supported in the agricultural segment of our economy as the years go by.
The third problem is that of larger productive units. The manufacturing industry across the nation is realizing that as this competition becomes more severe we will have to reorganize our economy into larger productive units. The small secondary industry may very well become somewhat irrelevant in the kind of trading competition we will have to face in certain areas of our secondary manufacturing. If this type of merger takes place without those affected feeling that it is taking place within the pattern of a plan, I am afraid this will be done only with the opposition of either management or labour because neither will have the assurance that they will benefit from the advantage of these large units.
The fourth problem upon which I wish to touch is that of retraining and education. We have really just begun to scratch the surface of the problem of retraining our people. We have come to the conclusion that we have tragically failed the youth of our nation over the past fifteen years. We have been supplying our need for skilled workers from immigration sources, bringing in people to do the jobs for which we should have been training our own people. We have made a start in this area but surely it is only a start. Unless we make some important changes in our economy I do not believe we can achieve the kind of dynamic results which must take place if we are to provide our younger people with the educational goals they require.
The European common market is not only planning economically but it is planning educationally. It is providing opportunities for young people to move from nation to nation. It is arranging for the acceptance of credentials of training between nations. This is the situation with which we have to compete. People will be able to take their skills back and forth among the nations. It is more than economic planning with which we must deal.
Our young people are very discerning in this area. You do not have to spell it out to them that we do not have any plan or national goal. They feel we are a society of drift rather than a society of decision. As

a result too many of our young people have no goals and drop out when it seems convenient, perhaps through discouragement. As I say, we have made a start in this area of providing training but much remains to be done.
In the last 12 months we have experienced less immigration to Canada than emigration from this country. Some 70,000 persons came to Canada and approximately 73,000 or more went out. It is tragic to note that many who are leaving are among those who have received training in skills in Canada. This outflow must be stopped. It can be done only through establishing and achieving national goals and objectives.
Many speakers on the government side have appropriately shown enthusiasm about the pick-up in our economy. In 1962 we see an increase in our gross national product. We have made some advances in the area of trade. But I suggest this is the time we need planning the most. Now that the economy shows an upward trend we must ensure that it does not fall, with the disastrous results we have witnessed in the past. It will be of no value if this climb in the economy should be followed by a sharp decline within three or four years.
In the past we have turned to scapegoats. We have blamed labour for wages. We have blamed the Liberals for what they did prior to 1957. We may begin to blame the European common market. Perhaps in the future we may blame the communist bloc. But we cannot continue to find scapegoats. The government must accept the inevitable responsibility of the challenges of this era. We must not allow this to be simply a cancerous affluence followed by a disastrous depression. Only in a planned economy can we create taxation policies which will encourage and assist an ordered growth. Only then can we direct investment, both private and public, into those areas that will provide the kind of full employment which the Canadian people have a right to expect and indeed will expect in the next decade.
Our economy is enjoying an upswing but I suggest this is the time to discipline ourselves and provide the opportunities presented by the twentieth century, which we have claimed as our own. One of my favourite historians is Arnold Toynbee. His thesis is, of course, that every civilization rises and falls. He might bring this thesis into the area of the nation state. Every nation faces certain challenges. If it overcomes those challenges, it continues to rise, to prosper and to provide something meaningful within western civilization. If it fails to meet those challenges, then indeed it has no right to expect anything else but a falling down in its prosperity and influence throughout the world.

We in Canada face many ills. There is still squalor in our major cities. There is still ignorance. It is not illiteracy but rather an inability to meet the challenges of the technological age. There is still unemployment, as we have seen even in this winter of upswing. There are still people who are not being cared for properly and who are in sickness and in want. These are the challenges of the 20th century and of the 20th century nation state.
I think the realities are just as stark for the nation state as they are for civilization. With the knowledge we have in this world of science and technology, with our ability to send a man around the world in space and to produce machines which can carry out production for us, we have the opportunity of making a nation worthy of all our hopes while on the other hand our technology and our machines can bring tremendous unhappiness. This is the challenge. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that the amendment to the amendment which we in the New Democratic party have proposed can give in the national government the planning and the policies which can bring about the affluence and progress which all Canadians desire.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to discuss a grievance. My grievance is provoked by a procedure that was followed by a minister in this house which I consider is an invasion of the rights of parliament and an abuse of authority which reflects

on the very basis of our method of enacting laws in this House of Commons. I refer to the statement on immigration made to the house by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mrs. Fairclough) shortly after this house opened, the effect of which is to make new immigration laws which the elected representatives of the people have had no opportunity to debate.
I find no precedent for a government dealing so evasively with such a serious matter when a different course had been promised, not only to parliament but indeed to the people of Canada. The production of a new set of immigration regulations instead of a revision of the Immigration Act is, I consider, an affront to the rights of parliament, to the press of Canada and indeed to the people of the entire country. It is nothing more in my judgment, than an attempt to divert the country's attention, and a poor demonstration of a lack of courage to face an issue. It is a move, a clumsy move at that, to block a parliamentary debate on the immigration laws of this country.
The chronological history of events of this whole manoeuvre shows that this government and the minister on at least nine different occasions clearly stated a promise to revise the Immigration Act. Not once was anything said about revising or altering the regulations themselves. I should like to refer to only two brief quotations in this regard. One appeared in the Ottawa Citizen of August 11, 1961 and is as follows:
Canada's new blueprint for immigration, four years in preparation, will make its debut in parliament next month.
A government spokesman said Thursday it is "absolutely sure" that the new Immigration Act will go before the Commons shortly after it reconvenes September 7. It had been forecast in the speech from the throne that opened parliament in November, 1960.
The document has been promised by the Conservatives since before they came to power in June, 1957 but delay after delay has kept it from being introduced.
The second quotation is from the Toronto Globe and Mail of November 2, 1961, and is as follows:
The final draft of Canada's revised Immigration Act, in the government's oven for many months, is now being considered by the cabinet. Full approval is expected soon and the revised act should be before parliament at the next session. Completion of the final draft marks the end of months of discussion and argument within the cabinet and the Department of Citizenship and Immigration. Revisions to the act were forecast in the speech from the throne a year ago, but they were not forthcoming.
The Prime Minister has himself on a number of occasions promised that the act would be revised. I want to put on the record one of these direct statements. I quote from the Toronto Star of May 15, 1961, which quotes
Alleged Abuse of Immigration Regulations from the Prime Minister's speech at Massey hall in April, 1957. This is the brief quotation:
"We will overhaul the act's administration to ensure that humanity will be considered and put an end to the bureaucratic interpretations which keep out from Canada many potentially good citizens", said Mr. Diefenbaker, at Massey Hall in April, 1957-
The minister herself very definitely told the house that she would make available a draft of her new legislation to interested groups before it was formally presented to parliament. I quote her own words:
I do not want to bring in a half-baked piece of legislation which will not stand the test of time.

I submit that the minister did not bring a half-baked measure before the house: I think it is a completely raw measure. It represents a raw deal not only to the house but to the country.
The minister did not introduce the piece of legislation promised by herself and the Prime Minister. She brought forward immigration laws which were not passed by parliament. These are purely and simply immigration laws passed by the cabinet. The representatives of the people have not had an opportunity to express an opinion on those laws, those regulations which are now considered to be the laws of this country. She failed to submit those regulations to interested groups as she promised she would. But, of course, that was only another promise. What is one broken promise more or less to members of the government?
I point out that this is legislation by ministerial regulations. If you care to think back in history, that is the way dictators operated. That is the way this government is operating. That is not a good method to be followed by the government of any country, particularly a democratic country. There is nothing more undemocratic than to make laws by ministerial regulation without giving the elected representatives of the people an opportunity of discussing them. A frightful danger of delegating authority is that it can lead to the making of laws under the guise of regulations.
On a previous occasion I complained as I complain now that the authority given in a parliamentary statute to make regulations has unfortunately degenerated to the point where officials and bureaucrats are carrying things a little too far.

speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman permit a question? Would he inform the house when the power to pass these regulations was included in the act? Was this not done under a Liberal administration?
I could not tell the hon. gentleman when it was done.
Oh, oh.

Just a moment. When an hon. member asks a question I expect that he and those who support his party will have the patience and courtesy to listen to the reply. I do not know when it was done. I am not

attempting to conceal when it was done. Regardless of when it was done, that does not make it right, unless hon. members opposite are prepared now to make the statement that everything the Liberal administration did was right. If they make that statement, then I would go along with it; but I do not take the position that if it was done by a Liberal government it is necessarily right.
I am raising a grievance. The system of delegating the authority to make regulations under the statutes is a good thing. Regulations have to be made for administrative purposes. But an abuse occurs when that authority is converted into the making of laws.
I have no quarrel with any statute that gives authority to a minister or commission to make regulations. That is the language of the statutes. The making of regulations is appropriate, proper and necessary for various branches of government. But an abuse takes place when laws are enacted under the guise of regulations. That is going too far.
Lord Hewart, a chief justice of England, has written and spoken extensively on this form of making laws by bureaucratic operation. Hon. members will recall the quotation from the Prime Minister's speech at Massey hall in which he said he would stop this form of bureaucratic law making. I have merely paraphrased his comment. He made reference to "bureaucratic" practices.
Lord Hewart calls this form of law making by bureaucratic operation the "new despotism". I sincerely commend Lord Hewart's book to all members of the house. His Lordship points out that the authority given to statutory bodies and government departments to make laws by regulation places government departments above and beyond the sovereignty of parliament itself, and frequently even beyond the jurisdiction of the courts.
What do we see? This delegation of authority is very dangerous. The Prime Minister himself has recognized the danger. On one occasion he spoke about appointing a committee or commission to review all our statutes and the attendant regulations enacted thereunder and determine whether the regulations were abusive and inconsistent with the bill of rights, an infringement on the rights and duties of parliament itself. That is a statement which the Prime Minister made or one to that effect. It was quite a proper statement and one becoming a prime minister, especially at a time when we were discussing the bill of rights. Unfortunately, however, no such commission has been appointed or set up. I simply say that was perhaps just another promise which the Prime Minister
Alleged Abuse of Immigration Regulations made and which I still hope he will fulfil. I consider the matter to be an extremely important one which is basic to our whole system of government and to our system of making laws, namely that there should be no such abuse by statutory bodies making laws instead of regulations.
As I said, if such a commission is ever formed, I feel that the greatest offender will be found to have been the regulations made under the Immigration Act. On another occasion I will point out many basic errors, contradictions and inconsistencies in the regulations themselves and even, to a large extent, their complete futility. What the minister has so far done by her surprising and astounding performance is to lead the house, the press, the country and future immigrants down the proverbial garden path. Under the guise of regulations she virtually shoved down the throat of parliament without debate, as a & fait accompli, a new set of immigration laws. She promised a revision of the act, but that was only another promise.
I should like to point out that a revision of the act would make possible debate, study by a committee, submissions by interested parties, analysis, discussion and amendments so that in the final analysis, out of all this consideration which is generally given to a piece of legislation in this house could come a better measure. I should like to feel that had these regulations which the minister brought into the house been given to a committee and to the house for debate, whoever it was who fashioned those regulations might have received enough suggestions, good or bad, to produce-to use the minister's language-a better seasoned measure or a better seasoned product, in her desire to produce for the country something that was good, properly cooked and digestible.
I feel that this whole operation over the past four years by the government and by the minister, this build-up of a promise to revise-"Later", "not quite ready", "I want to have the bill ready and distributed to interested parties to study"-was nothing but a hoax. All that did not happen. Nothing like that was done. The entire build-up to me has the air of a huge hoax on the country and on parliament. I say that is a genuine grievance. I feel that it is the result of a studied plan by the minister and by the government to string the country along and then to come and throw into the records a set of immigration laws in the guise of immigration regulations. I say that Canadians do not like to be treated in that way. I say that Canadians will resent being treated in that way. If the government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration had
1330	HOUSE OF
Alleged Abuse of Immigration Regulations the courage to make this promise that they would revise the act, they should have gone along with the revision properly and should not have slipped into the records in this devious or indirect way a series of immigration laws. 1 repeat that Canadians do not like to be treated in that way. They resent such treatment and they will show their resentment at the first opportunity given to them.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak on the grievance that is before the house at this moment, particularly as I represent a constituency composed of a great many people who have recently come to Canada. I know they would wish me to say on their behalf how much they disagree with the words which have just been uttered by the hon. member of the Liberal party. He said the Conservatives promised to revise the Immigration Act.
Did they not do so?
Of course they did so.

I am not concerned with that matter. I am concerned, as are the people who wanted to come to Canada, with the previous 22 years when revision of the act was wanted by these people who could not get into Canada then but who got into Canada under a Conservative government.
I am also concerned, Mr. Speaker, with the plaque that is hanging on the walls of this parliament building. Perhaps the hon. member has not seen it. Perhaps he will go and look at it some day. It is a plaque which was donated to the government of this country, the first one to accept tubercular refugees under the United Nations program. Has the hon. member seen it? I will show him where it is in the morning, Mr. Speaker.
It is wonderful to hear these people in the opposition talking about the immigration regulations and laws of this country. What do they know about the immigrants who have come to this country?
They practically all came here when the Liberal government was in power.
Certainly they did.
Just look at the statistics.

They came when there was in power a government which had a policy of Canadian babies first, and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate (Mr. Pickersgill) can substantiate that statement: Canadian babies first.
We let the immigrants in. You have kept them out.
Obviously he was the youngest one in his family.

It is quite
obvious that the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate might have been writing speeches in the last few days. He might have written this one. I do not know. However, I and the new Canadians in my constituency know of the policy under the previous government. 1 will point out two facts. This Conservative government was the first government of this country to recognize the refugee problem.
That statement is not correct.
Oh, oh.

It is not correct.
Mr. Pallet!: The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate can make his own speech.
Who admitted the Hungarians?
My hon. friend can talk about the Hungarians on his own time. However, I think that also happened after 1957.
No. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was the minister.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was also the advocate of Canadian babies first.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to tell the house that in my constituency I have a great many people who have recently come to Canada. They came here under various circumstances. Some of them came here under the refugee program instituted by this government with respect to people with tuberculosis in the refugee camps. They came here because they believe in democracy, because they believe in our way of life. They did not come here because of the policies put forward by our predecessors in office. They wanted an opportunity to be equal; they did not want to be considered inferior.
On a point of order, Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member for Port Arthur is rising on a point of order.

It seemed to me that the grievance of the hon. member for Cartier related to the introduction of regulations to change immigration policy. There are a number of us who wish to speak on this matter, and I would put it to you, sir, that the hon. member who is speaking has not been directing his remarks to the specific grievance.

speechtext: Perhaps I should hear the hon. member who has the floor on the point of order.

Mr. Speaker, in my view the grievance that was introduced covered a wide field. I do not think it was necessarily confined to immigration regulations but rather covered the whole field of immigration into Canada. I think there were statements made by the member who raised the grievance that had nothing to do with the regulations at all. I will await your ruling.

On the point of order, Mr. Speaker, at least at one point in the remarks of the hon. member for Cartier it was clear that he was directing his criticism at the activities of the former minister of citizenship and immigration, the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate, particularly when he was referring to the principle of incorporating regulations as part of a statute. Unless I greatly misunderstood the hon. member, that was his point. As the hon. member for Bona-vista-Twillingate was responsible as the former minister of citizenship and immigration for such regulations being imposed, my impression was that at least part of the criticism of the hon. member for Cartier was directed at the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
On the point of order, Mr. Chairman-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. It is not necessary to hear the hon. member. Having followed the hon. member for Cartier through his entire speech, I understood him to say that he was not attempting to deal with the content of the law but that his grievance related to the method of introducing immigration law by regulation rather than by statute, and I think that the comments of other members should be limited to the grievance as it was initiated.

Mr. Speaker, I will conclude by saying that in my estimation and that of a great many members of this house the official opposition is not in
Alleged Abuse of Immigration Regulations favour of the change in the regulations. They want to restrict immigration into Canada as it was restricted under the former government. We all know that was detrimental to those people who wanted to come to this country, to live in a democracy under a government freely and democratically chosen.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to exercise the right that you accorded to me to make a factual correction in the statement made by the hon. gentleman. The hon. member stated that this government was the first government that had paid any attention to the refugee problem or had admitted refugees. That statement is completely and utterly incorrect. In the years before the war the government of Mr. Mackenzie King undertook to admit refugees. After the war there was a very large refugee program and, as the hon. member has said, I was brought into this personally.

Mr. 1332	HOUSE OF
Alleged Abuse of Immigration Regulations

Mr. Speaker, as a member of the house who over the years has had to deal with a vast number of immigration cases and in whose riding are thousands of new citizens I am particularly interested in the grievances raised by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). That grievance has to do with important changes in immigration policy being brought in by regulation and not through the medium of legislation.
The hon. member for Cartier pointed out that in his view a great number of Canadians were and are very much disturbed by this situation and the procedure followed, and I believe he is correct in that statement. In my opinion the matter was very properly put by Michael Barkway in an article in the Ottawa Citizen of February 5. Because his words are concise and go to the root of the grievance I should like to quote a few sentences. He said in part:
The greatest change in immigration policy since Mackenzie King announced the resumption of immigration in 1947 has gone into effect without approval or even debate in parliament. The essence of it is to give immigration officials greater responsibility and more individual discretion than they have ever had before-
The reason why such a fundamental change of policy could be made without parliament's approval is that the real control over immigration has always been at the cabinet's discretion. The Immigration Act in practice leaves the government free to do almost anything it wants.
In those words I think we have the crux of the situation, and the correctness of that view was very definitely expressed in the words of the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration when she made a statement on January 19 of this year. In opening her statement on the change in immigration policy by regulation the minister put the matter in these words:
The new regulations are in two parts, the first of which has been formally approved by the governor in council as P.C. 1962-86 of January 18, 1962, while the second part requires only the approval of the minister under section 62 of the Immigration Act. These new regulations consolidate, revise and replace the various regulations passed in previous years, including those issued under previous ministerial authority.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I should like particularly to draw the attention of the house to the next sentence in the minister's statement.
Part I of the new regulations deals with such important questions as visa requirements, admissible classes, the responsibility of transportation companies and most of the major administrative and policy matters dealt with in the present regulations.
So, Mr. Speaker, I think it is a fair assumption to make from the words of the minister, uttered on January 19, that by regulation and by regulation only, will the major
[Mr. Pickersgill.l

administrative and policy matters in relation to immigration be decided. These matters will not be decided by the people of Canada through their representatives in parliament, but will be decided by the minister in charge at the time or by the cabinet. I say, sir, that the hon. member for Cartier has a rightful grievance because the particular principle involved here is whether we, in this country, in matters of such importance as immigration, will be governed by legislation or by regulation. In other words, is the major policy going to be laid down by order in council or by legislation enacted by the representatives of the people? Are we going to have policy and administration by order in council?
This is a subject, sir, upon which a great deal has been said in the past, but apparently it has to be said again. The meaning of democracy is rule by parliament so far as is humanly possible, not rule by order in council. We heard from the member for Cartier and the speaker who followed something of what the present administration has done through regulation, and something of what the previous administration did or did not do. One reason we have this situation is rule by order in council in the field of policy rather than through legislation. Perhaps, sir, I could just give one example that comes to my mind because the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate mentioned the refugees. I seem to remember some rather big headlines this hon. member got when he occupied the position of minister of citizenship and immigration at the time of the Palestinian refugee problem. The former minister, on behalf of Canada said, because Canada was interested in these one million Palestinian refugees, that Canada would be glad to make a contribution by having some of these people. However, he laid down two regulations they had to meet. They had to be able to speak either English or French and they had to have a skill. Although the principle was sound, to the best of my knowledge there were not any of these refugees who came to Canada, because they could not meet the regulations. This was one regulation that was laid down.
When the minister made her statement on January 19 she referred to the order in council of January 18 establishing the new regulations. If you examine them carefully, Mr. Speaker, I do not believe you will find very much difference compared with the previous regulations as to who may come in, how they may come in and the basis upon which they may come in. We have gone too far by regulation instead of legislation, and it is now beyond the power of the administration to handle appeal matters and correct grave injustices. It is as a result of this that

we have run into all these complaints, all of these disputes, all of these unhappy things that have developed in Canada and which have been discussed outside of Canada.
I feel, sir, it is because of this attitude of cabinet or ministerial control on such important matters that we have had situations such as the disgraceful manner in which the Chinese problem was handled when we asked that group to be stool pigeons-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order; the hon. member is now going beyond the scope of the subject under discussion.
I understood that was done by regulation.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member is not free to discuss everything that has been done by regulation. It is a very simple and neat point, namely that this change in the law was brought about by regulation rather than by statute.

Of course, I always bow to your views in matters of this nature, Mr. Speaker. I come back to whether or not it is proper to establish by regulation what should be the will of the people with regard to immigration policy. We in this group feel very strongly that when it comes to matters of policy, whether it is immigration or anything else, that is something which, in the ultimate, should be the subject of legislation and not regulation. This is particularly true when we consider that for months, even years, we were told there were going to be changes in the Immigration Act itself. We were told for years that not only the regulations but the legislation were under review.
All of us, sir, were definitely of the opinion that there were going to be major changes made by the present Minister of Citizenship and Immigration, but by legislation. It is understandable, therefore, that we in the house, and the people of Canada as a whole, fail to understand this important announcement of January 19 conveying information about new laws in connection with immigration. These matters were not going to be referred to parliament, because they had already been decided on the previous day by the cabinet. The new law had been enacted by order in council. I suppose, sir, we should have been most happy at the courtesy and kindness of the government in informing us the day after of the action which they had taken. I say there is a very important principle involved here, and that is rule by law or rule by regulation; rule by the people's will by legislation or rule by order in council.
This is a matter upon which one could speak for a long time. However, I am aware of the fact the minister desires to make a
Alleged, Abuse of Immigration Regulations contribution to this debate, and it is only right and just that I should leave some time available for her. I think I have made the point clear so far as this group is concerned. We believe in parliamentary democracy and not cabinet dictatorship.

speakeroldname: Hon. Ellen L. Fairclough (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration):
speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in replying to the previous three speakers, may I first of all say a word with regard to refugees. I do not believe that either this government or the previous government can lay claim to being superior to each other in the matter of the treatment of refugees. Canada has an excellent record in this field, quite the best of any country in the world.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
I, as the present minister, am very proud of it, and I am sure the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) is proud of it as the previous minister. When I occasionally see articles referring to the remarkable record of other countries in the alleviation of distress among refugees I am sometimes forced to smile at the naivete of the persons who write these articles and who speak on the subject from public platforms when in actual fact they haven't a clue what they are talking about.
Canada has taken in a great many refugees on a great many occasions. I was in this house at the time the former minister made his announcement with respect to Hungarian refugees, and I know he will agree with me that there was not a dissenting voice here.
That is right.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
We supported the proposal to bring these unfortunate people to Canada and to do what we could to rehabilitate them. I may say that their record here has been an excellent one. I am also personally proud of the record that has been established by the tubercular refugees who came to Canada. I am proud of the part that the various provinces took in caring for these people, in cooperating with the federal authorities in seeing that they should have proper treatment and that their families could be cared for until the breadwinner, if it were he, or the person who was afflicted, was able once more to take his or her place within the family circle.
Having said that I should like to make a few remarks with regard to the allegations- if I may call them that-which have been made by the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl). I was intrigued by his introduction of the subject, wherein he talked about the various promises that had been made, and then quoted from two newspapers. If I can

Alleged Abuse of Immigration Regulations read my shorthand notes-I used to write shorthand but I am afraid I am a little rusty- the first article he read I believe referred to a quotation from the Ottawa Citizen. The second article, without identifying any person, did not go so far as to say that information had been gained from any official government source, but just speculated there would shortly be forthcoming a revised act.
I believe I made it clear during the last few months that what would be brought forward would probably not be a new act because * we ran into difficulties in attempting to revise the act. As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) can appreciate, it is much easier to be more restrictive in drawing legislation than it is to be more flexible, and that was partially the problem which confronted us. Anyway, the hon. member for Cartier said I had intended to wait until I could bring in not just a piece of legislation, not just a half-baked piece of legislation. That is quite correct and that is still my intention. I might say he would have been better advised to follow the same example in his speech.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Sit down.

speechtext:
I have only a few minutes and I would prefer to finish.
I might ask the question: since when did a Liberal government submit regulations for any legislation to parliament for debate? I cannot recall regulations being submitted to parliament for debate either under this or any other legislation. The regulations are made according to the authority given to the governor in council under the required legislation, and under the governor in council the government of the day takes responsibility for drawing up those regulations and presenting them to parliament.
But the Prime Minister promised to change all that.
Another interruption.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: As a matter of fact I am sure that hon. members of the house will realize, as I have, that apparently both opposition parties were well aware that this subject was to be raised. I was not myself, of course, and therefore, Mr. Speaker, I must speak more or less from the few notes I have been able to make while listening to this criticism.

speakerposition: Minister of Veterans Affairs; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: Your speech is better than his.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
But if my memory serves me well, the former government declared in a speech from the throne in 1951 that it

would revise the Immigration Act. Nothing was done. Again, in 1952 they repeated this intention-
It was revised.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: -and that year they finally did bring in a revised act; but that act, although passed, was not proclaimed.
What?

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: The following year nothing was said about it, but it eventually was proclaimed and became law, I think late in 1953; again, if my memory serves me well, it was September. That act was brought in. It is true that it was presented to this house for consideration; but when was it presented? It was presented in the dying days of a session and crammed through this house, with little or no time provided to give proper consideration to an extensive act which contained some 74 clauses. Now criticism is being levelled at a government which is attempting in an orderly fashion to bring in legislation affecting people who desire to enter Canada, and affecting their relatives and friends who are in this country.

Nothing done in four and a half years.
Mr. Pallet!: Tell us about 1919 and hospital insurance.
That is the record.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The minister has the floor.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, these interruptions do not bother me at all; in fact, I find them rather amusing. I do not wonder that hon. members in the opposition benches become a little irked at their ineffectual criticism of legislation brought down by this government, because they cannot help but think back to those long years of inactivity when they sat on this side of the house; and now, of course, every month seems like a year to them.
Oh, oh.
And to the public.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
It was said by the hon. member for Cartier that the people of this country had been led up the garden path. I believe those were the words he used. Mr. Speaker, contrary to his belief, the suggestions which came to my desk from many bodies were carefully considered in the drafting of these regulations. These suggestions came from church groups, religious groups, social service bodies, immigrant aid societies and from some of the hon. member's own close friends. He
does not like the regulations. I wonder why, because some of his colleagues outside this house like them. I have had letters to that effect-quite a number of them. I suggest the reason the hon. member does not like them is because they please people too well.
I have no intention of allowing myself to be stampeded into bringing in legislation prematurely, regardless of the howls from the opposition benches. They can shout their heads off from now till doomsday, I will bring in my legislation when I am ready to bring it in.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Minister of Citizenship and Immigration
speechtext:
I might say this. I have been the minister of this department now for something less than four years and I have been engaged in the study of a revision of this act for something approaching two years. I have received representations from various groups. Those representations were not that this government should hurry and bring in a new act, but quite the reverse: the representations from these groups were, "Go slowly. Do not be too quick in this matter. Give us a chance to talk to you about it". That we have done.
I should have liked to bring in a new act complete with regulations at one time, but it became evident very soon in our study of the act that this was probably not a wise course. Therefore we took the alternative, and we have brought in regulations, which I submit to this house are workable, flexible and will permit the entry of many persons who were heretofore denied entry to Canada.
I think it was in 1959-I hope, Mr. Speaker, that I will not be quoted on this as a statement of fact, because I am depending on my memory-that we admitted some 7,000 persons to this country by order in council because they did not qualify for entry under the old act or the old regulations. This is a rather ridiculous situation when there are so many persons who are welcome to Canada by reason of their peculiar circumstances or qualifications but who are prohibited from entry because of the legislation which is in effect. We believe that with the new regulations we have cured that situation.
I might say that it is still my intention to consult with the various bodies who are interested-those I have mentioned, the immigrant aid societies and religious groups, who have always worked closely with the department-but before doing so we believe we should give these regulations a few months to work, to see what will happen and whether there are perhaps some flaws in them which need to be corrected.

The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch), who I know has been keenly interested in immigration matters and has made representations to my department on countless occasions on behalf of various persons, has said that there is too much done by regulation and not enough by legislation. Mr. Speaker, the hon. members of this house would not want everything spelled out by legislation. Half the hon. members of this house are constantly applying to my department for the exercise of ministerial discretion with regard to cases where people would not be admissible under the regulations. If we are going to tie it down so tightly that everyone is admissible through the act, then I submit that very few people will get into this country.
We wish to give these regulations a chance to work, as I have said, and I can assure the house that I intend to proceed in an orderly fashion. I hope I will have the co-operation of members of parliament in seeing that when the act is revised it meets their wishes and the wishes of the people of Canada.
Before the hon. lady takes her seat-
Ten o'clock.

Before the hon. lady takes her seat would she permit me to ask her a question? Is it not correct that in 1957 before the election the Prime Minister promised to revise the act and that that has not been done?
It will be.
